primitives.name: McDiarmid's inequality (bounded-differences concentration, Theorem D.8)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem D.8 (McDiarmid’s inequality) Let X1, . . . , Xm ∈Xm be a set of m ≥1 independent random variables and assume that there exist c1, . . . , cm > 0 such that f : Xm →R satisﬁes the following conditions:
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: S=(X_1,...,X_m): i.i.d. sample, m a dimensionless count; X_i in arbitrary measurable space X (no units); f:X^m->R a real statistic carrying whatever unit the observable has (probability in [0,1] for error rates, bits for information statistics); c_i>0: per-coordinate bounded-difference constant, SAME unit as f; epsilon>0: deviation threshold, same unit as f; E[f(S)]: expectation, same unit as f; LHS is a probability, dimensionless in [0,1]; exponent 2*epsilon^2/sum(c_i^2) is dimensionless (unit^2/unit^2), so the bound is dimensionally homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: As printed: X_1,...,X_m independent (m>=1); f satisfies the bounded-differences condition |f(...,x_i,...)-f(...,x_i',...)|<=c_i for ALL i and ALL points x_1,...,x_m,x_i' in X; c_i>0 deterministic constants. No identical-distribution requirement beyond independence; no continuity or convexity of f.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when any coordinate influence is unbounded (c_i=+infinity makes the exponent 0 and the bound vacuous at 1); fails under dependence between X_i (the Doob martingale proof requires independence to telescope conditional expectations); the two-sided form needs both tails, one-sided Lipschitz control only gives one tail; heavy-tailed f with rare large jumps violates the uniform bounded-differences premise even if the variance is small (use Bernstein/Bennett instead, exercise D.6).
timescales: tau_0: single-coordinate perturbation (one observation swapped)
tau_1: aggregation over m independent observations
tau_2: confidence calibration at failure probability delta
tau_3: re-estimation when the sampling regime drifts (independence breaks)

layer2.mapping: Binds as a confidence CHANNEL on any aggregate football telemetry statistic computed over m independent drive-level observations: if replacing one drive changes the statistic by at most c_i (e.g. per-drive EPA share, success-rate indicator in [0,1] with c_i=1/m), the season aggregate concentrates around its mean with exponential tails. This is the audit kernel that turns noisy per-drive observables into a calibrated state estimate with an explicit deviation budget epsilon; it is a Layer-2 isomorphism of the concentration inequality, NOT a claim that the theorem originated in football.
layer2.telemetry: Per-drive outcome indicators bounded in [0,1] (success flag, EPA sign), drive count m, empirical leave-one-drive-out deltas used to estimate c_i; deviation epsilon set from the decision's risk budget. All observables are internal tracking/charting data, never sportsbook odds.

primitives.name: Rademacher generalization bound (Theorem 3.3)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 3.3 Let G be a family of functions mapping from Z to [0, 1]. Then, for any δ > 0, with probability at least 1 −δ over the draw of an i.i.d. sample S of size m, each of the following holds for all g ∈G:
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: G: family of functions g:Z->[0,1] (losses or indicators, dimensionless probability units); z~D a random example, S=(z_1,...,z_m) i.i.d. sample, m dimensionless count; E[g(z)]: true risk, probability units; (1/m)sum g(z_i): empirical risk, same units; R_m(G)=E_S[sup_{g in G}(1/m)sum sigma_i g(z_i)] expected Rademacher complexity with sigma_i uniform in {-1,+1}, same [0,1] units; Rhat_S(G) empirical Rademacher complexity, same units; delta in (0,1) failure probability, dimensionless; every additive term is in [0,1]-compatible units so the inequality is dimensionally homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: As printed: G maps Z to [0,1] (bounded loss); S drawn i.i.d. of size m; bound holds uniformly for ALL g in G simultaneously with probability >=1-delta. The empirical version (3.4) replaces R_m by the data-dependent Rhat_S at the cost of the constant 3 and log(2/delta). Proof applies McDiarmid to Phi(S)=sup_g(E[g]-Ehat_S[g]) with bounded difference 1/m.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Vacuous when R_m(G) does not decay with m (e.g. G shatters arbitrarily large sets, infinite VC-dimension such as the sine family of example 3.16); unbounded losses violate the [0,1] premise and need truncation or relative-deviation bounds; the uniform guarantee collapses if the sample is not i.i.d. (the McDiarmid step fails); for data-dependent model selection the empirical complexity must itself be estimated, adding a second concentration layer.
timescales: tau_0: one sample draw S of size m
tau_1: empirical-risk computation over S
tau_2: complexity penalty estimation (Rademacher averages)
tau_3: model-selection horizon where capacity must shrink as data accumulates

layer2.mapping: Derived selection kernel for the Coach-Mind hypothesis class: when choosing among play-call prediction models of differing capacity, the bound supplies the penalty term 2*Rhat_S(G)+3*sqrt(log(2/delta)/(2m)) that must be added to empirical fit before any model is trusted out-of-sample. It binds to the model-selection CONSTRAINT in the simulation: a high-capacity deception model that fits the training log perfectly is vetoed unless its Rademacher penalty is paid. Layer-2 derived kernel, not a football origin claim.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical 0-1 loss of each candidate model on m logged plays; empirical Rademacher complexity estimated by sign-flip resampling of the play log; delta fixed by the decision risk budget. Inputs are internal charting/tracking logs only.

primitives.name: Representer theorem (Theorem 6.11)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 6.11 (Representer theorem) Let K : X × X →R be a PDS kernel and H its corresponding RKHS. Then, for any non-decreasing function G: R →R and any loss function L: Rm →R ∪{+∞}, the optimization problem argmin h∈H F(h) = argmin h∈H G(∥h∥H) + L �h(x1), . . . , h(xm)  admits a solution of the form h∗= Pm i=1 αiK(xi, ·). If G is further assumed to be increasing, then any solution has this form.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: K:X x X->R a positive definite symmetric (PDS) kernel, units of the RKHS inner product; H the corresponding reproducing kernel Hilbert space with norm ||h||_H (units sqrt(kernel)); x_i in X observed sample points (e.g. formation feature vectors, dimensionless after normalization); alpha_i in R dual coefficients (units of h divided by kernel units); G:R->R non-decreasing regularizer acting on the norm; L:R^m->R union {+infinity} loss on the m evaluations h(x_i) (units of h); h* the minimizer, same units as h. The expansion is an equality in H, hence dimensionally homogeneous term by term.
primitives.assumptions: As printed: K is a PDS kernel with RKHS H; G non-decreasing; L any loss function (possibly +infinity, enforcing constraints). If G is strictly increasing then ANY solution has the finite expansion form. The proof uses the orthogonal decomposition H=H1 direct-sum H1-perp with H1=span{K(x_i,.)} and the reproducing property h(x_i)=<h,K(x_i,.)>.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The finite-span conclusion requires the regularizer to depend on h ONLY through its RKHS norm and the loss ONLY through the m evaluations; adding a term that probes h off-sample (e.g. a derivative penalty at unseen points) breaks the theorem; indefinite (non-PDS) kernels have no RKHS and the decomposition fails; with G merely non-decreasing a solution exists in the span but non-span solutions may also exist; numerical breakdown when the kernel matrix is near-singular (duplicate or near-duplicate x_i).
timescales: tau_0: one training sample of m formations
tau_1: kernel matrix assembly K(x_i,x_j)
tau_2: regularized fit producing alpha_i
tau_3: out-of-sample evaluation h*(x)=sum alpha_i K(x_i,x)

layer2.mapping: Isomorphism for the defensive-response function class: any norm-regularized response model in the RKHS of a formation-similarity kernel is a weighted combination of responses anchored at OBSERVED formations (the support points x_i with alpha_i != 0). This binds the transition kernel of the Coach-Mind sim: the learned response to a new formation is interpolated from kernel-weighted historical responses, and the support set identifies which historical looks actually carry the model. Layer-2 isomorphism of the representer theorem; the theorem itself is pure kernel-methods mathematics.
layer2.telemetry: Formation feature vectors x_i from internal charting; PDS kernel matrix K (e.g. Gaussian on normalized formation features); fitted dual coefficients alpha_i and their sparsity (support count); leave-one-out response deltas. No odds inputs.

primitives.name: AdaBoost empirical-error bound (Theorem 7.2)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 7.2 The empirical error of the classiﬁer returned by AdaBoost veriﬁes: bRS(f) ≤exp  −2 T X t=1 1 2 −ϵt 2 . (7.3) Furthermore, if for all t ∈[T], γ ≤ � 1 2 −ϵt  , then bRS(f) ≤exp(−2γ2T) . (7.4)
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Rhat_S(f): empirical 0-1 error of the boosted classifier f on sample S, dimensionless probability in [0,1]; epsilon_t: weighted training error of the base classifier h_t at round t under distribution D_t, dimensionless probability in [0,1]; gamma: edge, dimensionless, gamma=min_t(1/2-epsilon_t) in [0,1/2]; T: number of boosting rounds, dimensionless count; exponent -2*sum(1/2-epsilon_t)^2 dimensionless; Z_t=2*sqrt(epsilon_t(1-epsilon_t)) the normalization factor, dimensionless. All terms dimensionless probabilities; homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: As printed: AdaBoost with alpha_t=(1/2)log((1-epsilon_t)/epsilon_t), distributions D_{t+1}(i)=D_t(i)exp(-alpha_t y_i h_t(x_i))/Z_t; the bound uses 1_{u<=0}<=exp(-u) and 1-x<=exp(-x). The second form requires a uniform edge gamma<=1/2-epsilon_t for ALL t in [T]. The algorithm need not know gamma (it adapts).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Vacuous when any epsilon_t>=1/2 (edge<=0: a base learner at chance or worse contributes nothing and the exponent stops growing); with random classification noise the edge collapses and convex potential boosters provably fail (Long-Servedio, chapter notes); the bound is on TRAINING error only - generalization needs the margin bound (theorem 5.8 / chapter 7 margin analysis); numerical overflow of exp(alpha_t) when epsilon_t->0.
timescales: tau_0: one boosting round t (fit h_t, reweight)
tau_1: T-round ensemble accumulation
tau_2: margin/generalization calibration after training
tau_3: deployment drift where the weak-learner edge decays

layer2.mapping: Derived ensemble kernel for situational prediction: combine T weak situational classifiers (down-distance, field-zone, personnel-group tendencies) into one strong predictor; the bound says the training error decays exponentially in the accumulated squared edge sum(1/2-epsilon_t)^2. It binds to the ENSEMBLE-WEIGHT transition in the Coach-Mind sim: each round's weight alpha_t is set by its calibrated edge, and a round whose edge is zero is automatically neutered. Layer-2 derived kernel; boosting's origin is computational learning theory (Freund-Schapire), not football.
layer2.telemetry: Per-round weighted error epsilon_t on the reweighted internal play log; edge gamma_t=1/2-epsilon_t; round count T; resulting empirical error of the ensemble. Calibration uses charting/tracking labels only, never sportsbook lines.

primitives.name: Uniform-stability generalization bound (Theorem 14.2)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Then, with probability at least 1 −δ over the sample S drawn, the following holds: R(hS) ≤bRS(hS) + β + (2mβ + M) s log 1 δ 2m .
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: R(h_S): true risk of the hypothesis returned by algorithm A trained on S, units of the loss L (probability for 0-1 loss); Rhat_S(h_S): empirical risk, same loss units; beta: uniform stability coefficient, sup over samples S,S' differing in one point and over z of |L_z(h_S)-L_z(h_S')|, same loss units; M: bound on the loss, 0<=L<=M, same loss units; m: sample size, dimensionless count; delta in (0,1): failure probability, dimensionless; the sqrt term is dimensionless so (2m*beta+M) carries loss units, matching R and Rhat. Dimensionally homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: As printed (theorem 14.2, pp. 351-352): loss L bounded by M>=0; A is (uniformly) beta-stable; S is m points drawn i.i.d. from D. The proof applies McDiarmid (theorem D.8) to Phi(S)=R(h_S)-Rhat_S(h_S) with bounded difference beta+M/m. The text notes beta=o(1/sqrt(m)) is necessary for the bound to converge, and beta=O(1/m) holds for regularized ERM (section 14.3).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Vacuous when beta does not decay faster than 1/sqrt(m) (the (2m*beta) term then dominates); unstable algorithms (e.g. unregularized nearest-neighbor or sparse selection, cf. Xu-Mannor-Caramanis chapter notes) have beta=Theta(1) and the bound gives nothing; unbounded losses violate the M premise; non-i.i.d. samples break the McDiarmid step; beta itself is algorithm-dependent and must be proven, not assumed.
timescales: tau_0: single-game perturbation (leave-one-game-out)
tau_1: m-game training aggregate
tau_2: generalization-gap certification at delta
tau_3: regime shift where stability coefficient must be re-measured

layer2.mapping: Isomorphism for game-plan generalization: a plan fitted on m logged games generalizes to a new opponent iff removing any ONE game changes the per-play loss by at most beta. This binds to the ROBUSTNESS CONSTRAINT on the Coach-Mind sim: leave-one-game-out loss deltas are the stability telemetry, and a plan whose deltas exceed the beta budget is flagged as overfit to a single opponent's tape. Layer-2 isomorphism of the stability bound; the theorem is pure learning theory (Bousquet-Elisseeff lineage).
layer2.telemetry: Leave-one-game-out empirical loss deltas (estimate of beta); loss bound M from the loss definition; game count m; held-out opponent loss as the R(h_S) proxy. Internal game logs only.

primitives.name: Q-learning convergence theorem (Theorem 17.18)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 17.18 Consider a ﬁnite MDP. Assume that for all s ∈S and a ∈A, P+∞ t=0 αt(s, a) = +∞, and P+∞ t=0 α2 t(s, a) < +∞with αt(s, a) ∈[0, 1]. Then, the Q-learning algorithm converges to the optimal value Q∗(with probability one).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Q_t(s,a): state-action value at epoch t, units of expected discounted reward (reward units, e.g. points or a dimensionless utility); r(s,a): immediate reward, same reward units; gamma in [0,1): discount factor, dimensionless; alpha_t(s,a) in [0,1]: step size, dimensionless; s,s' in S states, a,a' in A actions (finite sets, counts dimensionless); the temporal-difference bracket has reward units, multiplied by dimensionless alpha, added to Q in reward units: homogeneous. The step-size conditions are dimensionless series constraints.
primitives.assumptions: As printed: FINITE MDP; for all s,a the Robbins-Monro conditions sum_t alpha_t(s,a)=+infinity and sum_t alpha_t(s,a)^2<+infinity with alpha_t in [0,1]; these impose that every state-action pair is visited infinitely often. The proof (pp. 417-418) rewrites the update as stochastic approximation of H(Q)(s,a)=r(s,a)+gamma*E_{u~P[.|s,a]}[max_a' Q(u,a')], shows H is a gamma-contraction in ||.||_infinity, and invokes theorem 17.17 (supermartingale convergence).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails for infinite/continuous state-action spaces without function approximation (and with approximation, the text warns of cycling, section 17.5.6); fails if any (s,a) is visited only finitely often (the series conditions cannot hold there); gamma->1 slows the contraction (running time not polynomial in 1/(1-gamma), footnote 24); non-stationary environments violate the fixed-MDP premise; the convergence is asymptotic (probability one), giving no finite-sample rate (see Even-Dar-Mansour, chapter notes).
timescales: tau_0: one transition (s,a,r,s') and TD update
tau_1: epoch of visits ensuring exploration
tau_2: contraction-driven convergence of Q to Q*
tau_3: policy deployment where the environment may drift (MDP premise breaks)

layer2.mapping: Derived policy-value kernel for sequential play-calling under an UNKNOWN transition model: the call-selection policy is the greedy argmax_a Q(s,a) where Q is learned by stochastic approximation of the Bellman fixed point, with state s = (down, distance, field zone, score differential, time) and reward = expected points added. The gamma-contraction is the transition-kernel regularizer that makes the value iteration well-posed; the visitation condition is the exploration constraint. Layer-2 derived kernel of Watkins' Q-learning; no football origin is claimed for the theorem.
layer2.telemetry: State-action visit counts n_t(s,a); step sizes alpha_t=1/n_t(s,a) (satisfy the series conditions); TD error delta_t=r+gamma*max Q(s',.)-Q(s,a); discount gamma fixed by the possession-value horizon. All from internal play-by-play and tracking, never odds.

reasoning_traces.think: Extraction reasoning for Foundations of Machine Learning, second edition (Mohri, Rostamizadeh, Talwalkar, MIT Press 2018), book_id 192267e30813837d, 505 pages read in full. The book is a graduate learning-theory monograph, so the sovereign primitives must be theorems with exact hypotheses, not algorithm recipes. I selected six kernels that span the book's proof architecture: McDiarmid's bounded-differences inequality (appendix D, p. 459) is the concentration engine; the Rademacher generalization bound (theorem 3.3, p. 48) is the capacity-control engine; the representer theorem (theorem 6.11, p. 134) is the kernel-methods engine; the AdaBoost empirical-error bound (theorem 7.2, p. 166) is the ensemble engine; the uniform-stability bound (theorem 14.2, pp. 351-352) is the algorithm-dependent generalization engine; and Q-learning convergence (theorem 17.18, p. 416) is the sequential-decision engine. The deliberate choice is that these are not independent results: the book's own proofs wire them together. Theorem 3.3 is proven by applying McDiarmid to Phi(S)=sup_g(E[g]-Ehat_S[g]) with bounded difference 1/m (p. 48, equation 3.6). Theorem 14.2 is proven by applying McDiarmid to Phi(S)=R(h_S)-Rhat_S(h_S) with bounded difference beta+M/m (p. 352, equation 14.1). Q-learning convergence is proven by showing the Bellman operator H is a gamma-contraction in the infinity norm and invoking the supermartingale convergence theorem 17.17 (pp. 417-418). So the dependency graph is: concentration (p1) -> uniform capacity control (p2) and algorithmic stability (p5); contraction (p6) -> sequential value learning; the representer theorem (p3) reduces infinite-dimensional RKHS optimization to m coefficients; AdaBoost (p4) is the margin/ensemble specialization. Every verbatim quote was sliced programmatically from the whitespace-normalized pymupdf dump and asserted to be a substring of the cited page, so no quote is hand-transcribed. Each LaTeX field uses the book's own notation (Rhat_S for empirical risk, R_m for Rademacher complexity, beta for stability coefficient, gamma for both the discount factor and the boosting edge - the book reuses gamma, so the ledger disambiguates per primitive). The unit ledgers check dimensional homogeneity: concentration exponents are unit^2/unit^2, risk bounds add terms all in loss units, and the Q-update adds reward-unit quantities scaled by dimensionless step sizes. I also confirmed the book reuses the symbol gamma in two distinct roles - the boosting edge in theorem 7.2 and the MDP discount factor in chapter 17 - so each ledger pins gamma to its local definition to avoid a cross-primitive unit collision. Breakdown regimes are taken from the printed hypotheses and the book's own caveats: unbounded coordinate influence kills McDiarmid; infinite VC-dimension (the sine family, example 3.16) kills the Rademacher decay; non-PDS kernels kill the representer expansion; zero edge kills AdaBoost; beta not o(1/sqrt(m)) kills the stability bound; finite visitation kills Q-learning. Layer-2 mappings are explicit isomorphisms or derived kernels into the 22-player football dynamical system, with calibrating telemetry drawn only from internal charting, tracking, and play-by-play logs. No football origin is fabricated for any theorem: these are pure mathematics and computer science, and the Layer-1 invariant is the source theorem itself. No sportsbook odds appear anywhere as a model input, per the held-out discipline.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The hidden state of this book is a century of scars about overfitting. The lineage runs from Vapnik-Chervonenkis (1971) uniform-convergence theory, through Valiant's (1984) PAC model, to the realization that distribution-free VC bounds are too pessimistic for real data, which motivated data-dependent Rademacher complexity (Bartlett-Mendelson 2002, cited p. 461). McDiarmid's (1989) bounded-differences inequality descends from Hoeffding (1963) and Azuma (1967) martingale work; the book notes the exponent improvement by a factor of four (p. 445). Boosting descends from Schapire's (1990) strength-of-weak-learnability and Freund-Schapire (1997) AdaBoost, with the margin explanation of Schapire-Freund-Bartlett-Lee (1997). Stability-based generalization descends from Kearns-Ron (1999) and Bousquet-Elisseeff (2002). Q-learning descends from Watkins (1989) and the Robbins-Monro (1951) stochastic-approximation lineage. Each primitive carries that scar: the bound exists because someone watched a model fit noise and demanded a certificate.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Recursive belief clash under pressure: the head coach's comfort call is a low-capacity hypothesis chosen to minimize regret against the defensive coordinator's perceived tendency, while the DC's tendency trap is a deliberately planted pattern that exploits exactly that low-capacity comfort. The quarterback's internal clock is a third belief model - a timing policy trained on practice reps that may not match the live pass rush. The Rademacher lens (p2) says the coach's comfort model must pay a capacity penalty before it is trusted; the stability lens (p5) says if removing one week of tape flips the call, the call is overfit to a single opponent look. Modeling the DC as modeling the coach modeling the DC produces the recursion: the trap only works if the coach's hypothesis class is small enough to be shatterable by a few looks, which is precisely the condition the capacity bound quantifies. The QB's clock is the exploration policy that must keep visiting all state-action pairs (p6) or the value estimate collapses.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Cross-layer veto adjudication: a high-EV call can be vetoed by physics or psychology even when the learned value Q(s,a) is large. Physics veto: if the pass-rush time-to-pressure telemetry makes the QB's internal clock infeasible, the Q-value computed under an assumed pocket-collapse time is invalid - the transition kernel premise (p6) is violated, so the call is vetoed regardless of EV. Psychology veto: if the coach's comfort call is a stability-zero artifact (leave-one-game-out delta exceeds beta, p5), the apparent edge is an overfit and is vetoed. Concentration veto: if the per-drive influence c_i is unbounded (a single broken play dominates the statistic, p1), the confidence interval is vacuous and the EV estimate cannot be certified. The adjudication rule is: a call proceeds only if the capacity penalty is paid (p2), the stability budget holds (p5), and the physical transition premise is satisfied (p6); otherwise the high-EV number is rejected as uncertified.

reasoning_traces.think: Second-pass reasoning: verification and binding. I re-read the proof dependencies to confirm the six primitives compose rather than merely coexist. The composition is a certificate pipeline. Step one: raw per-play or per-drive observables are bounded (0-1 indicators or bounded EPA shares), so McDiarmid (p1) gives an exponential deviation budget for any aggregate. Step two: when the aggregate is a supremum over a hypothesis class, the bounded difference is 1/m and the deviation budget becomes the Rademacher generalization bound (p2), which is the model-selection constraint. Step three: when the aggregate is the generalization gap of a specific algorithm, the bounded difference is beta+M/m and the budget becomes the stability bound (p5), which is the robustness constraint. Step four: the hypothesis class itself, if it is a regularized RKHS, collapses to m kernel coefficients by the representer theorem (p3), which is what makes the capacity penalty computable from data. Step five: an ensemble of weak predictors built on that class has training error controlled by the accumulated squared edge (p4). Step six: if the decision is sequential rather than one-shot, the value function is the fixed point of a gamma-contraction and is learned by stochastic approximation (p6). The critical invariant across all six is that every certificate is only as strong as its weakest premise: independence for p1, boundedness for p2, PDS for p3, positive edge for p4, decaying beta for p5, infinite visitation for p6. I verified each quote against the normalized dump and each ledger for dimensional homogeneity. The Layer-2 bindings are deliberately conservative: they map theorems to constraints, channels, and transition kernels in the football simulation, and they name the telemetry that would calibrate each binding, while explicitly refusing to claim any football origin for the mathematics. This is the honest posture the contract demands: Layer-1 is the source invariant, Layer-2 is the explicit mapping, and the telemetry is internal-only. Before any of this I performed the mandatory page-one retraction check: the title verso, MIT Press title page, and series page carry no publisher retraction notice, and the text is internally coherent (the proof dependencies above cross-check without contradiction), so the source qualifies for COMPLETE rather than INSUFFICIENT_SOURCE_ACCESS. Had a retraction DOI or an equation contradicting an earlier equation appeared, the honest outcome would have been refusal, not extraction.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The genealogy of the certificate pipeline is the history of statistical learning trying to escape worst-case pessimism. VC theory gave distribution-free guarantees that were too loose to explain practice; the scar was that practitioners ignored the bounds. Rademacher complexity and stability theory were the response: data-dependent and algorithm-dependent certificates that could actually be computed. The representer theorem made kernel methods tractable by reducing infinite dimensions to a finite support. Boosting turned the weak-learnability question into a constructive margin machine. Q-learning turned stochastic approximation into a model-free controller. Each step exists because the previous certificate was either too weak to trust or too expensive to compute, and that pressure is the hidden state this extraction preserves.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The second-pass theory of mind models the analyst who must present a call to the coach. The analyst believes the high-EV number; the coach believes the comfort call; the DC believes the trap. The analyst's recursive task is to anticipate the coach's reaction to a certificate that contradicts comfort. If the analyst presents only the EV, the coach defaults to comfort (a low-capacity prior). If the analyst presents the stability delta and the capacity penalty, the coach can see WHY the comfort call is overfit. The QB, meanwhile, models the analyst modeling the coach: if the QB expects the comfort call, his internal clock is calibrated to that timing, and switching to the certified call breaks his timing unless the transition premise is re-checked. So the certificate must be presented together with its physical feasibility, or the human layer vetoes it.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Second-pass veto: the composition itself can be vetoed. If the observables are not independent (drives within a game are correlated by game script), McDiarmid's independence premise fails and the entire certificate pipeline downstream is uncertified - this is the most common real-world failure and must be flagged before any EV is trusted. If the kernel is indefinite (a similarity score that is not PDS), the representer reduction is invalid and the capacity penalty cannot be computed. If the environment is non-stationary (opponent adjusts mid-game), the fixed-MDP premise of Q-learning fails and the learned Q is stale. The adjudication rule: check the premises in dependency order (independence -> boundedness -> PDS -> edge -> stability decay -> visitation), and veto at the first broken premise rather than propagating an uncertified number.

universal_lens: A polymath audit lens for any learned decision system: every certificate decomposes into (1) a concentration engine bounding deviation of bounded-influence aggregates, (2) a capacity or stability penalty that must be paid before out-of-sample trust, and (3) a contraction or fixed-point premise that makes sequential value learning well-posed. Audit by checking the weakest premise first; a high expected value with a broken premise is uncertified, not clever.
gsi_mapping: Mapped to GSI clinical and bioenergetic telemetry as an explicit isomorphism, not a claim about the book: McDiarmid (p1) bounds deviation of bounded per-trial physiological aggregates (e.g. per-rep heart-rate or force-plate indicators); the stability bound (p5) certifies that a dose-response or rehab model fitted on m sessions generalizes when leave-one-session-out loss deltas decay; Q-learning contraction (p6) is the template for adaptive training-load policies under unknown athlete response dynamics. Axonal-shear and fluid-bioenergetic models supply the bounded observables; the theorems supply the confidence and robustness certificates. No physiological origin is claimed for the mathematics.
gse_mapping: Mapped to GSE Coach-Mind simulation, deception, and DFS/portfolio tail risk as explicit Layer-2 kernels: the Rademacher penalty (p2) is the model-selection constraint on deception and tendency models; the representer theorem (p3) reduces formation-response models to a support set of historical looks; AdaBoost's edge (p4) weights the situational ensemble; stability (p5) flags game plans overfit to one opponent; McDiarmid (p1) gives tail-risk deviation budgets for portfolio aggregates; Q-learning (p6) is the sequential call-value kernel. All telemetry is internal charting/tracking/play-by-play; no sportsbook odds are used as inputs, and nothing here is published.
